messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled

Vignette:
Margaret is a 78-year-old White American woman who has spent decades working as a public defender, a role that has kept her moving through courthouse hallways, jail interview rooms, parking structures, and city streets with the brisk competence of someone used to handling conflict. She is married and had long thought of herself as practical, unflappable, and hard to intimidate. The assault that now occupies so much of her attention happened after an ordinary workday, in a setting that had once felt routine. She had left the courthouse carrying a worn leather case and headed toward her car as evening was coming on. In the parking area, she became aware of someone behind her only a moment before he was upon her. The attack was sudden and close; what stayed with her was the shock of another person appearing in her space without warning, the sense that she had not had time to prepare, and the immediate calculation that she could be seriously harmed. In the midst of it she was acutely aware of footsteps, movement at her back, and the impossibility of knowing what the man would do next.

In the weeks that followed, Margaret returned to work because she took pride in not being “the kind of person who gives in,” but her days no longer unfolded with their old automatic ease. Walking from the courthouse entrance to her office, she found herself repeatedly turning to look over her shoulder. At first she told herself she was simply being careful. Then it became something she did almost constantly: in elevators, in the corridor outside arraignment court, crossing to the employee lot, even while unlocking her office door. If she heard footsteps that matched her pace, her neck and shoulders tightened before she had fully registered why, and she would look back quickly to make sure no one was closing in on her. She described it as feeling foolish and absolutely necessary at the same time. What frightened her most was the idea of being caught unaware again.

Her work environment sharpened this vigilance. As a public defender, she spends her days among distressed family members, detained clients, corrections officers, prosecutors, and strangers waiting outside courtrooms. She now watches people closely in a way she never used to. In crowded courthouse lines she studies faces, hands, posture, and tone, scanning for any sign that someone may turn aggressive. If a man lingers too near her in the hallway or shifts his weight in a way she cannot immediately read, she becomes fixed on him until she can decide whether he is a danger. She has noticed herself choosing seats in conference rooms with a clear view of the door and hesitating before stepping into stairwells unless someone else has already gone through. She does not describe these actions as habits so much as rules she has come to rely on. From her perspective, this is what sensible people do after learning how quickly ordinary surroundings can become unsafe.

The jumpiness has been especially distressing because it feels out of proportion to the moment and unlike her. A file dropped unexpectedly in chambers, a voice raised behind her, the sudden opening of a secure courthouse door, or her husband entering a room before she has heard him approach can make her whole body jerk. She hates how visible this is. She has spent a career projecting steadiness in adversarial settings, and now younger attorneys sometimes notice when she startles at small noises. Once, when a client’s family member moved abruptly beside her at counsel table, she recoiled so sharply that she had to pause before continuing the conversation. She later found herself preoccupied not only with the incident but with who may have seen it.

At home, the same pattern follows her into ordinary life. In grocery store aisles she checks behind her when a cart rolls up too quickly. On evening walks with her husband, she keeps track of who is approaching from the rear and may ask to cross the street without explaining why. If someone comes up behind her while she is getting into the car, her heart lurches before she can reassure herself that nothing is happening. Her husband has noticed that she sits in restaurants facing the room and that she studies other patrons with a guarded, appraising look. Margaret knows this has narrowed her world, even if she does not frame it that way. It takes more effort to get through a day that used to feel familiar.

What finally brought her to seek help was not a dramatic crisis but the accumulating strain of living in this state of alertness. After being startled in the courthouse garage by a colleague calling her name from behind, she found herself shaken enough that she waited in her car for several minutes before driving home. She began to wonder whether this constant readiness was becoming the organizing fact of her days. She came to treatment still committed to her work and still unwilling to be defined by what happened, but she was candid about her fear: that she will never again feel safe when someone is behind her, and that the professional life she has built so carefully will continue to be overshadowed by the expectation that danger can appear at any moment. At the same time, she is hoping, quietly but firmly, that she might learn how to move through her own city without scanning every face and every footstep.
